title: This eel got eaten alive, then escaped through the gills

qwen_instruct.narrator: Gripping, punchy storyteller narrating a wild true nature story. Fast and energetic, dramatic on the big moments.
qwen_instruct.eel: A small, cheeky, sarcastic cartoon creature. Quick and squeaky.
qwen_instruct.scientist: An astonished scientist watching a monitor, half whisper, half gasp.

lines.text: This eel just got eaten alive. And it's about to escape, through the fish's gills.
Meet a baby Japanese eel. Tiny, slippery, and on the menu.
This is a dark sleeper. It doesn't chew. It swallows prey whole.
One lunge, and the eel is gone. Straight down, into the stomach.
It's dark, it's tight, and it only has a few minutes.
Scientists in Nagasaki, Japan, wanted to see what happens next. So they filmed it on X-ray.
Inside the stomach, the eel swims in circles, hunting for a way out.
Then it finds the tube it came down, jams its tail in, and reverses. Backwards, up the throat, towards the gills.
And out of the gill, pops a tail.
Of thirty-two eels swallowed, thirteen got their tails out, and nine escaped completely. On average, in fifty-six seconds.
It's the only fish ever confirmed to escape from a predator's stomach.

experiment.hypothesis: Remake of 013 in the fast-cut set style: cold open on the tail poking out of the gill, a cut every ~2 s across three sets (riverbed, inside the stomach, X-ray lab), an on-screen escape timer, character lines for the eel and a scientist.

facts.claim: Hasegawa et al. (Nagasaki University), Current Biology 2024: juvenile Japanese eels injected with barium sulfate were filmed on X-ray video after being swallowed by dark sleepers (Odontobutis obscura).
Of 32 eels that reached the stomach, 28 tried to escape; 13 got their tails out of a gill and 9 escaped completely, in 56 seconds on average.
Eels moved back up the oesophagus tail first towards the gills; some circled the stomach first, apparently searching for a way out.
Eels that failed to escape stopped moving after roughly two and a half to three minutes in the stomach.
Hasegawa: the Japanese eel is the only fish species confirmed to escape from a predatory fish's digestive tract after capture.
